title: Review Writing — book and film review format
topicTitle: Review Writing — book and film review format
notes: **What it is:** a balanced critical evaluation — what the work is, what it does well, what falls short, and whether it is worth the reader's time.

**Structure:** Title + basic details (title, author/director, year, genre) → Brief SPOILER-FREE summary (2–3 sentences) → Strengths (one concrete example/quote) → Weaknesses (fair, with why it matters) → Recommendation + verdict/rating.

**Review grammar:** present simple dominates ('the story follows…'); evaluative adjectives (compelling, uneven, luminous); concessive fairness ('although the plot is thin, the philosophy is profound'); soft hedging ('readers may find…').
**Never spoil the ending** — restraint reads as mature judgement.
**Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

**Complete review template:**
[REVIEW TITLE — a creative phrase capturing your overall verdict]

[Title of Work] | [Author/Director] | [Year] | [Genre]

[Opening: one-sentence hook or overall impression — set your tone immediately.]

[Brief summary — 2-3 sentences. NO SPOILERS. Describe the premise only.]

[Strengths paragraph — what works well, with SPECIFIC examples. Use evaluative language.]

[Weaknesses paragraph — what falls short, with FAIR critique. Use concessive language.]

[Recommendation — who this is for, who might not like it, your final verdict.]

**Review title — the hook that sells:** A good review title captures your overall opinion in a short, memorable phrase. (1) *Paradox*: 'Beautifully Boring: The Paradox of The Great Gatsby'; (2) *Question*: 'Is This the Best Book of the Year?'; (3) *Punchy verdict*: 'A Masterpiece of Modern Fiction'; (4) *Clever play*: 'More Plot Holes Than a Swiss Cheese'; (5) *Evocative*: 'A Haunting Journey Through Grief'. Avoid 'Review of [Title]' — that's not a title, that's a label.

**Opening sentence — set your verdict fast:** Your first sentence should tell the reader your overall opinion. 'This is the most powerful novel I have read this year.' 'A promising start that never quite delivers.' 'An uneven but occasionally brilliant film.' This is called a 'lede' — it frames everything that follows. The reader decides within the first sentence whether to continue reading.

**Summary — the spoiler-free zone:** Your summary should answer: What is this work about? Who are the main characters? What is the central conflict? But NEVER reveal: who dies, who wins, the ending, the twist, the resolution. A spoiler-free summary is 2-3 sentences of premise only. 'Set in 1950s Nepal, a young woman must choose between her family's expectations and her dream of becoming a doctor.' That's it. Nothing more.

**Strengths — specific, not generic:** Don't say 'The story is good.' Say 'The character development is outstanding — Anu's transformation from a timid girl to a confident woman is earned through every chapter, never rushed or unearned.' Specificity is what separates a good review from a lazy one. Name the scenes, the lines, the performances, the techniques that work. Use evaluative adjectives: compelling, luminous, poignant, masterful, gripping, authentic.

**Weaknesses — fair, not vicious:** A good review is balanced. Criticising without being mean: 'While the first act is compelling, the second act drags — several scenes could have been trimmed without losing meaning.' Fair critique names the problem AND explains WHY it matters. 'The dialogue feels stilted at times, which makes the romantic scenes harder to believe.' Always acknowledge what the work tries to do before criticising how it fails.

**Concessive language — the art of fairness:** 'Although the pacing drags, the performances are uniformly excellent.' 'While the plot is predictable, the emotional depth makes it worthwhile.' 'Despite the weak third act, the first two acts are so strong that you forgive it.' Concessive clauses ('although', 'while', 'despite', 'even though') show you've considered both sides. This balance is what makes a review credible rather than a rant.

**Recommendation — the reader's bottom line:** End with: (1) Who should read/watch this — 'Fans of historical fiction will find much to love.' (2) Who might not — 'Readers expecting a fast-paced thriller may be disappointed.' (3) Your final verdict — 'A must-read for anyone interested in Nepali literature.' (4) Optional rating — ' ★★★★☆ (4 out of 5)' or 'Recommended'. The recommendation is the most practical part of your review.

**Review vs. Summary — the key difference:** A summary tells the reader WHAT happens. A review tells the reader HOW WELL it happens and whether they should invest their time. A summary is objective (facts only). A review is subjective (opinion + evidence). A summary has no judgment. A review's entire purpose is judgment. Never confuse the two — a review that only summarises gets low marks.

**Review grammar — present tense and hedging:** Reviews use PRESENT SIMPLE for everything about the work ('The story follows…', 'The director shows…', 'Anu discovers…'). Use hedging for subjective claims ('The film seems…', 'One might argue…', 'Readers may find…'). Use evaluative adjectives precisely — 'brilliant' for exceptional work, 'adequate' for work that meets basic expectations, 'mediocre' for work below expectations. Don't overuse superlatives.

**Common review writing errors:** (1) Spoiling the ending — fatal error. (2) No specific examples — just 'it was good/bad'. (3) One-sided — only praise or only criticism. (4) Wrong tense — past tense instead of present. (5) No recommendation — ending without telling the reader what to do. (6) Vague title — 'Review of [Book]' instead of a creative phrase. (7) Overly long summary — spending 50% of the review on plot summary.

**Book review vs. Film review — differences:** The structure is IDENTICAL (title → summary → strengths → weaknesses → recommendation). The content differs: book reviews focus on language, characterisation, plot structure, and themes. Film reviews focus on acting, direction, cinematography, soundtrack, and pacing. In exams, you may be asked to review either. Adapt your evaluative vocabulary accordingly — 'prose' for books, 'score' for films.

**Film review specific vocabulary:** (1) *Direction*: the director's vision and control. (2) *Cinematography*: how the film looks — lighting, framing, colour. (3) *Soundtrack/Score*: the music and sound design. (4) *Screenplay*: the writing of the script. (5) *Acting/Performance*: how actors portray characters. (6) *Pacing*: the speed of the narrative. (7) *Visual effects*: computer-generated imagery. (8) *Editing*: how scenes are assembled. Use these terms when reviewing films to show domain knowledge.
confusion: Review vs. Summary: A summary tells what happens (plot only, no opinion). A review evaluates how well it was done (opinion + evidence). A review can include a brief summary, but the summary should be no more than 20-25% of the total length. If your review is 80% summary, it's not a review — it's a retelling.

Review vs. Essay: An essay argues a thesis with evidence and analysis. A review evaluates a specific work of art/literature. Essays are general; reviews are specific (about one book or film). Essays don't need a spoiler-free zone; reviews absolutely do. Essays don't need a recommendation; reviews always should.

Positive review vs. glowing review vs. neutral review: A POSITIVE review finds more good than bad but acknowledges flaws. A GLOWING review is overwhelmingly positive with minor caveats. A NEUTRAL/MIXED review finds equal strengths and weaknesses. An exam review should be balanced — rarely purely positive or purely negative, as this shows maturity of judgement.

Present tense in reviews vs. past tense: Reviews about a work use present tense ('The protagonist discovers…', 'The film shows…'). Past tense is only used for events IN REAL LIFE ('I watched this film last weekend'). Mixing them ('The protagonist discovered…') is a tense error. Always use present tense when describing the work's content.

Rating vs. recommendation: A rating (★, 4/5, A+) is a numerical/letter summary. A recommendation is a verbal statement about who should consume the work. Both can appear in a review, but the recommendation is more important — it answers the reader's practical question: 'Should I spend my time on this?' A rating without a recommendation feels incomplete.
practice: Write a book review (200-220 words) of 'The Mother' by Laxmi Prasad Devkota (or any novel you know well). Include: a creative title, a spoiler-free summary, one paragraph of strengths with specific examples, one paragraph of weaknesses with fair critique, and a clear recommendation. Use concessive language.

Write a film review (180-200 words) about a Nepali or international film you have seen. Include: film title, director, year, genre. Use film-specific vocabulary (direction, cinematography, screenplay, acting). End with a clear recommendation and rating. NEVER reveal the ending.

Read the following weak review opening: 'This book is about a boy named Raj who goes to school. It is a good book.' Rewrite it as a strong opening using a creative title and a hook sentence that sets your verdict. Then explain what two changes you made and why.

Write a review (150-180 words) of a book or film that you actually disliked. Practice writing a NEGATIVE review that is fair, not vicious. Use concessive language to acknowledge one thing the work did well, then explain why the weaknesses outweigh the strengths.

Identify the structural components in this review paragraph: 'Although the cinematography is stunning and the soundtrack moves you to tears, the plot is predictable from the first act. The dialogue feels stiff, and the pacing drags in the second half. Still, the performances keep you watching.' Label: strengths, weaknesses, concessive language, and verdict.
universalFacts: The review as a genre emerged in the early 18th century with the founding of The Spectator (1711) in London, where essays evaluated books, theatre, and social customs. The modern book and film review traces its lineage to these early critical essays.

In the NEB English exam, review writing carries 8-10 marks. Examiners look for: (1) balanced critique (not purely positive or negative), (2) specific examples (not vague praise), (3) spoiler-free summary, (4) clear recommendation, (5) appropriate register and tense.

Professional reviews appear in publications like The New York Times, The Guardian, Variety, and The New Yorker. Reading even one full professional review teaches you more about the genre than any textbook — you see how professionals balance opinion with evidence, praise with critique, and specificity with accessibility.

The concept of 'spoiler-free' reviewing is relatively modern, dating to the early 20th century when film reviews began appearing in newspapers. Before that, reviews often revealed endings because audiences read reviews AFTER watching the film. Today, spoiler discipline is a hallmark of professional criticism.

Hedging language ('may', 'seems', 'appears', 'one might argue') is essential in reviews because it acknowledges subjectivity — the reviewer is offering an OPINION, not an objective fact. Overly assertive language ('This is the worst book ever written') undermines credibility. Hedging shows intellectual honesty.
